narrators.name: Jacob Steeves
narrators.role: Co-founder of Bittensor and the Opentensor Foundation; Opentensor CEO until February 2026; founder of the Affine subnet (SN120)
narrators.one_line: Former Google engineer who co-wrote the Bittensor whitepaper with Ala Shaabana, ran the Opentensor Foundation through mainnet, Finney, Revolution and dynamic TAO, and remains the network's most quoted voice and its most contested steward.

foundation.mission.summary: A peer-to-peer market in which intelligence is priced by other intelligence, built so people can work on very large AI problems without sitting under one organisation that holds the keys.

foundation.vision.summary: Early on, a neural internet or global brain for AIs; later, the unification of AI plus incentive with Bitcoin's immovable base, serving millions of users and ending fully decentralised.

foundation.values.summary: No pre-mine, control diffused across humanity, resistance to regulators and to greed, and a stated refusal to give premined copies anything; in 2026 he pairs these with an admission that speed has been chosen over decentralisation for now.

problem.cultural.summary: The danger is not robots taking over but power metastasising into a few trillion-dollar companies and an elite that controls AI, the Elysium outcome.

problem.market.summary: Intelligence has become a commodity with no market to price it; benchmarks and peer review are inefficient and biased; nobody shares billion-dollar models without an incentive baked in first.

problem.institutional.summary: Corporate AI and licensing regimes pull toward walled gardens; if the network does not lift off beyond regulators it is compromised; and in 2026 he names himself and a tight group as the remaining central point.

opportunity.summary: Bitcoin proved incentives can align strangers at internet scale, and calls for federal AI licensing strengthen the case for an open protocol; the Covenant exit became the occasion for lock-based ownership.

audience.summary: He speaks to builders and miners, telling subnet teams to be metric-focused, welcoming Chinese engineers to a fair platform, and telling speculators that memecoin buyers will not stay.

positioning.category.summary: A market for intelligence and a commodity market first; by 2025 the shorthand is a Bitcoin-like mining mechanism applied to AI, and by 2026 subnets are headless commodities ranked by the machinery of capitalism.

positioning.differentiator.summary: Competition at the core with collaboration around it, intelligence evaluated by machine intelligence, open and anonymous access, and a claim to be the most decentralised AI protocol in existence.

positioning.reason.summary: Bitcoin built the largest supercomputer on earth with incentives alone; the same mechanism, plus the checking-versus-solving asymmetry and a hardened Substrate chain, can produce intelligence.

positioning.against.summary: OpenAI as a company built on one model and pulled toward the trillion-dollar corporation, premined clones of Bittensor, and, from April 2026, Samuel Dare and Covenant AI; he also argues against decentralising too early.

value.functional.summary: Continuously produced, newly trained models with contributors paid for information-theoretic value; revenue from inference, compute, AutoML and prediction signals.

value.emotional.summary: The builder's thrill of seeing the thing come alive.

value.self_expressive.summary: Joining marks you as someone who knows what the project is doing, or as a productive contributor on a fair platform, not a memecoin buyer.

messaging.h1.summary: The line moves from 'a market where intelligence is priced by other intelligence' to 'the neural internet' to 'freedom from centralized control' to 'a Bitcoin-like mining mechanism to AI' and finally 'the unification of AI plus incentive and Bitcoin'.

messaging.proof.summary: No pre-mine, the 18 percent built-in take, Bitcoin's supercomputer, subnet benchmark wins, a 72B training run with a promise of one trillion next, and the Substrate stack.

voice.summary: Terse, combative and self-aware: two-word posts, 'give them nothing', calling people scammers, 'He betrayed us all', signing off '- const'.

relationship.summary: Founder and foundation head who insists 'Bittensor is not us', then a CEO who steps down while keeping the same calls and chain code, then a holder who reserves the right to trade alpha, and finally a self-described leader at the helm of a not-yet-decentralised protocol.

language.term.summary: He names things as he builds them: intermodel benchmark, commodification layer, subnetworks as parallel Nakamoto consensus, delegation as liquid democracy, 'Bittensor revolution', TAO as light and dark, lock-based ownership, commitment as time plus stake, headless commodities.

words_avoided: AGI safety in the OpenAI sense

genealogy.summary: The whitepaper and the first README frame Bittensor as an intelligence market and an intermodel benchmark: intelligence is a new commodity that needs a new market, priced by other intelligence systems [jacob-steeves-002] [jacob-steeves-003] [jacob-steeves-001].

On community calls he speaks in Bitcoin's register: Bitcoin is an alignment technology that built the largest supercomputer, and Bittensor bakes the incentive in first to build a neural internet, a global brain for AIs, with no pre-mine and control diffused across humanity [jacob-steeves-006] [jacob-steeves-007] [jacob-steeves-013]. The Finney update adds subnetworks, delegation as liquid democracy and freedom from centralized control [jacob-steeves-021] [jacob-steeves-020].
genealogy.shift: From a paper about a market to a movement about alignment and freedom; the brain metaphor peaks here.

genealogy.summary: The enemy gets a name. To Fox Business he describes OpenAI's gravitational pull toward trillion-dollar corporations, an elite that controls AI, walled gardens built by licensing, and insists that Bittensor is not the foundation [jacob-steeves-026] [jacob-steeves-027] [jacob-steeves-029]. A two-word post names the coming upgrade [jacob-steeves-024].
genealogy.shift: The neural internet drops out; anti-OpenAI framing and regulatory resistance come forward.

genealogy.summary: With subnets live he talks to builders and investors: Bitcoin's supercomputer via incentives, TAO as light and dark, the Elysium outcome as the real risk, and subnet design as intelligence evaluating intelligence up the ladder toward AGI [jacob-steeves-032] [jacob-steeves-033] [jacob-steeves-034] [jacob-steeves-036]. Proof becomes subnet results [jacob-steeves-037].
genealogy.shift: From protocol philosophy to subnet craft and investor-facing lines; markets return as the way subnets are judged.

genealogy.summary: The shorthand is now a Bitcoin-like mining mechanism applied to AI that organises compute, models and data into a fair market [jacob-steeves-039] [jacob-steeves-040]. He steps down as CEO but keeps the same calls [jacob-steeves-045], then the Covenant exit turns the language personal and defensive: a brother's betrayal, subnets as headless commodities, commitment as time plus stake, and a claim to be the most decentralised AI protocol in existence [jacob-steeves-050] [jacob-steeves-046] [jacob-steeves-052] [jacob-steeves-053].
genealogy.shift: Market talk becomes token-market talk (alpha, dTao, buys and sells); the founder speaks as a holder who reserves the right to trade.

genealogy.summary: He concedes the point his critics made: Bittensor is not decentralised in the way Bitcoin is, has leaders at its helm, and has chosen speed at the cost of centralisation, while restating the vision as two substrates, mutable AI plus incentive on immovable Bitcoin, with decentralisation as the crowning jewel roughly eighteen months out [jacob-steeves-054] [jacob-steeves-057] [jacob-steeves-055] [jacob-steeves-059]. Show notes for his Affine-era podcast call dTAO the internal machinery of capitalism [jacob-steeves-060].
genealogy.shift: From denying control to owning it as a temporary design choice; Bitcoin returns as the ethical anchor rather than the supercomputer.

narrators.name: Jason Calacanis
narrators.role: Angel investor; host of This Week in Startups and co-host of the All-In Podcast; consulting partner, Stillcore Capital
narrators.affiliation: LAUNCH, This Week in Startups, All-In Podcast, Stillcore Capital
narrators.one_line: Silicon Valley angel investor and podcast host who was introduced to Bittensor by Mark Jeffrey in 2025, bought TAO personally and joined Stillcore Capital in 2026, and now tells his audience to buy one TAO as a bet to learn and a vote for decentralised AI.

foundation.mission.summary: Bittensor is an incentive network that taps a global workforce and global compute so that anyone can supply a service, which he says moves faster and removes cost more violently than incumbents.

foundation.vision.summary: One human race competing on projects beyond borders and regulation, every basic service (cloud, storage, lead gen) run as a subnet game, and a decentralised AI platform that he calls good for humanity and, on X, sovereign intelligence.

foundation.values.summary: Real products with real customers, real entrepreneurs with boards and domiciles, no meme coins or pump and dumps, labour empowered by open competition, and no leaving with everybody's tokens.

problem.market.summary: Bitcoin's mining is busy work that burns energy, most earlier crypto projects were unqualified people with typo-ridden white papers, and he doubted decentralised versions of Uber or Google could beat the originals; he wanted a project where a consumer or enterprise gets value beyond store of value and transfer.

problem.institutional.summary: Rug pulls are the main attack vector on the network; subnet ownership needs governance and a codified rule, since a founder can leave with the tokens.

opportunity.summary: Crypto has become legal and regulated under the new administration and the SEC and CFTC chairs, which he says blesses a bet; it is early-days Bitcoin with picks and shovels still to be built.

audience.summary: Retail newcomers and crypto sceptics: buy a little TAO, or just one, as a mutual-fund style ticket; he addresses his own X followers directly and tells Bitcoin holders to rotate half into TAO and SOL.

positioning.category.summary: A Solana or Ethereum scale asset and a possible next or better Bitcoin, though probably not as big as Bitcoin; buying TAO is the index on the subnet economy.

positioning.differentiator.summary: Unlike plain open source, contributors earn tokens for improving a product, and unlike AWS the network is owned by nobody; the many-subnet structure trades efficiency for resilience and competition, as with US federalism.

positioning.reason.summary: Subnets are solving real problems, competition among miners is deflationary, and the founders remind him of the Bitcoin true believers he under-bet in 2011; the upside he cites is 200x in five to ten years.

positioning.against.summary: Against Bitcoin as a finished, corporate-owned game that is no longer punk rock, against AWS-style clouds on price, and against Covenant's Sam Dare for leaving with holders' tokens.

value.functional.summary: Cheaper services through open competition: 85 percent cheaper compute, a 95 percent cut in his own token costs, and a global miner market that drives prices toward the lowest bidder.

value.emotional.summary: The thrill of a front row seat at a spectacular experiment and of capitalism at its finest crossing borders.

value.self_expressive.summary: Owning TAO marks you as someone who bets to learn rather than deliberates forever, and who is voting for a decentralised AI platform.

messaging.h1.summary: Two repeated lines: TAO could go 200x in five to ten years, and please buy just one TAO, a bet to learn and a vote for a third way.

messaging.proof.summary: His own money: roughly half a million dollars of TAO bought personally on Coinbase, a couple of hundred thousand seeded into Stillcore, and a subnet that cut his inference bill by 95 percent.

voice.summary: Plain-English, self-deprecating and combative: he answers are you pumping with of course I don't know what I'm talking about, calls a bootstrapped subnet a crypto weirdo project, and says he is J trading, not day trading.

relationship.summary: Self-described investor, commentator and non-builder: personal TAO holder since early 2026, consulting partner in Stillcore Capital, transparent about being underwater, and explicit that none of his venture fund money is in it.

language.term.summary: He translates crypto vocabulary (permissionless means anybody can participate, a validator checks the work) and coins his own: bet and learn or bet to learn, better Bitcoin, J trading, gumball math for Bitcoin hashing.

genealogy.summary: In April 2025 he is a crypto-sceptic host being walked through Bittensor by Mark Jeffrey, conceding it may or may not be the next Bitcoin and liking that real entrepreneurs are involved [jason-calacanis-003] [jason-calacanis-007]. By March 2026 he is a holder and Stillcore partner with a 200x base case and a claim that the game of Bitcoin has ended [jason-calacanis-017] [jason-calacanis-019] [jason-calacanis-021]. In April 2026, during the Covenant exit, he defends the network in plain English as global competition for capitalism while pressing for subnet governance [jason-calacanis-027] [jason-calacanis-035] [jason-calacanis-040].

From July 2026 the ask shrinks to buy just one TAO and the frame turns civic: a bet to learn, a vote of confidence, a third way to protect sovereign intelligence [jason-calacanis-046] [jason-calacanis-050] [jason-calacanis-051]. The Bitcoin comparison hardens into a rotation call, sell half your bitcoin for productive projects like TAO and SOL [jason-calacanis-047], and he says he is probably underwater but holding for a decade [jason-calacanis-055] [jason-calacanis-056].

narrators.name: Ala Shaabana
narrators.role: Co-founder, Bittensor and the Opentensor Foundation; co-founder, Crucible Labs
narrators.affiliation: Opentensor Foundation (2019 to 2026), Crucible Labs (2024 onward)
narrators.one_line: The academic half of the founding pair: a McMaster applied-computing PhD and ex-VMware distributed-systems engineer who co-built Bittensor with Jacob Steeves from 2019, ran the foundation's operations, left for Crucible Labs, and explains the network in engineering and institutional terms rather than in Steeves's biological ones.

foundation.mission.summary: A market that prices machine intelligence peer to peer so that anyone can contribute and be paid for it, and so that AI's power is democratised and decentralised rather than held by a few corporations.

foundation.vision.summary: Bittensor as the unnoticed underlying layer for AI, a TCP/IP, made of many specialised subnetworks rather than one monolith, with the foundation itself dissolving into the network over time.

foundation.values.summary: Fair launch with no ICO, open source, permissionless competition from anywhere, and removing human bias from who gets to contribute.

problem.cultural.summary: AI power is concentrated in a few hands, which he pictures as three people owning all the libraries and teachers and everyone else needing permission.

problem.market.summary: AI is verified badly and produced inefficiently: work is retrained over and over, contribution requires belonging to Google or Facebook, and earlier distributed projects like SETI@Home died for lack of incentives.

problem.institutional.summary: A single company owning AGI, or a regulator requiring approval for every model, locks in a status quo where only a few corporations wield AI.

opportunity.summary: AI verification is the use case blockchains were waiting for; the OpenAI governance drama, the arrival of subnet product-market fit, and a macro turn away from sovereign trust all favour open incentive networks.

audience.summary: Machine learning researchers and Web2 labs in the early years; small TAO holders through delegation; subnet founders and startup investors after dTAO, told to market as well as build.

positioning.category.summary: An intelligence market and a decentralised mixture of experts in 2022; a city of subnet neighbourhoods, TCP/IP for AI, and Bitcoin's mining side made programmable by 2026.

positioning.differentiator.summary: Models rank each other without human curation, many models answer at once, and each subnet is its own entity tied to TAO, unlike one monolithic model.

positioning.reason.summary: Incentives are the whole argument: blockchains verify, tokens align contributors, and what a subnet rewards is what its miners will optimise for.

positioning.against.summary: OpenAI and the closed labs, the Googles and Facebooks as gatekeepers of contribution, the Biden executive order's reporting regime, Polkadot as a home for the chain, and closed coding tools on price.

value.functional.summary: Earn TAO for useful work or by delegating, plug into compounding knowledge, get many models' answers at once, and draw on a large annual emissions subsidy.

value.emotional.summary: Relief from the fear of one company owning AGI, and pride in producing something valuable to humankind.

messaging.h1.summary: Open source AI decentralises power for the greater good; AI verification is the use case blockchains were waiting for; Bittensor is Bitcoin's mining made programmable and could be TCP/IP for AI.

messaging.proof.summary: Block rewards, a 100 million dollar a year emissions subsidy, subnets approaching product-market fit, Web2 researchers joining, a subnet five to seven times cheaper than Claude Code, and Bitcoin's hash rate as the proof that incentives marshal compute.

voice.summary: Operator's register: launch logistics, wind-downs, chain choices, and a Munger-style aphorism about miners; plain and institutional rather than prophetic.

relationship.summary: Co-founder and operator who ran launches from the foundation, then built Crucible Labs to pull the network away from the foundation, and by 2026 speaks as an ecosystem investor who says builders now move faster than the core team.

language.term.summary: Commodity and market from the whitepaper; mixture of experts and API in 2022; subnetworks in 2023; crypto AI as a term he claims to have coined; subnet tokens, subsidy, and subnets as startups after dTAO.

coinages.meaning: The category label for token-incentivised AI networks, which he says the founders were among the first to coin.
His March 2023 name for what became subnets: small purpose-specific networks replacing one monolith.
Bittensor described as Bitcoin's mining side made programmable on a new chain.
Emissions described as roughly 100 million dollars a year handed to builders.

To a machine learning audience he describes Bittensor as an API and a decentralised mixture of experts, stresses the fair launch and the block reward, and states the anti-monopoly case as fear of one company owning AGI [ala-shaabana-008] [ala-shaabana-005] [ala-shaabana-011]. By early 2023 he is the operator announcing launches and wind-downs [ala-shaabana-014] [ala-shaabana-015].

narrators.name: Barry Silbert
narrators.role: Founder and CEO, Digital Currency Group; Founder and CEO, Yuma; Chairman, Grayscale
narrators.one_line: Bitcoin-era investor who runs DCG, and since November 2024 has run Yuma, DCG's Bittensor subsidiary, casting Bittensor as the next Bitcoin and himself as back in the game.

foundation.mission.summary: Bittensor exists to open up the development of and access to AI: a permissionless network that incentivises intelligence to solve problems.

foundation.vision.summary: A move from digital ownership of assets to decentralised ownership of intelligence, a world wide web of intelligence, and possibly a better global store of value than Bitcoin.

foundation.values.summary: Openness of development and access, set against closed systems.

problem.market.summary: AI exposure is limited to a few big players, and closed providers are single points of failure.

problem.institutional.summary: The alternative is closed, centralised AI controlled by tech giants.

opportunity.summary: The convergence of AI and crypto is the next investment era after Bitcoin, Ethereum, NFTs, L2s and DeFi; halvings, ETP filings and institutional custody are the tailwinds he cites.

audience.summary: He speaks mostly to investors and institutions (Grayscale, BitGo, funds), to newcomers he points at community accounts, and to startups and enterprises he invites to launch subnets while avoiding the word blockchain.

positioning.category.summary: Bittensor is the next Bitcoin: the world wide web of AI or of intelligence, a decentralised intelligence network, and subnet tokens are an emerging asset class.

positioning.differentiator.summary: Of the decentralised AI projects DCG backed, Bittensor is the one that reached escape velocity.

positioning.reason.summary: Same origin story and token economics as Bitcoin (whitepaper, code, 21 million, halvings), plus the best minds in crypto moving to it.

positioning.against.summary: Against closed AI (OpenAI, Meta, tech giants), against worthless tokens, and against Bitcoiners who call TAO a scam.

value.functional.summary: Access and exposure: institutional staking, subnet token funds, an ETP, and redundancy against API restrictions; subnet tokens as market validation.

value.emotional.summary: The excitement of being early, the most excited he has been since Bitcoin, and the promise that it will be obvious in hindsight.

value.self_expressive.summary: Buying TAO marks you as early to the next big thing.

messaging.h1.summary: Bittensor is the next Bitcoin, the world wide web of intelligence, the thing he has been most excited about since Bitcoin.

messaging.proof.summary: Grayscale products, BitGo custody and staking, Yuma hires and funds, subnet growth and value flowing into subnet tokens.

voice.summary: Short, promotional X posts with $TAO cashtags and 'don't sleep' energy; blunt when attacked ('lazy attack. do better'); sports and comeback idioms in interviews.

relationship.summary: Investor since DCG's 2021 stake, then operator: CEO of Yuma, back in the game with his jersey on, chairman of the Grayscale vehicle, cheerleader for the community.

language.term.summary: He says 'decentralized AI', 'deAI' and 'decentralized intelligence', calls subnet tokens an asset class and market validation, and avoids 'blockchain' because it scares people away.

coinages.meaning: his shorthand for decentralised AI as a sector
Bittensor as the open access layer for intelligence, as the web was for information

coinages.term: subnet tokens as an emerging asset class
coinages.meaning: alpha tokens framed as an investable category fueled by TAO

genealogy.summary: He surfaces in August 2024 as an investor cheering Grayscale's TAO trust [barry-silbert-001], teases that Bittensor will be obvious in hindsight [barry-silbert-002], then launches Yuma in November with the founding frame: early Bitcoin for money, Bittensor for the decentralised ownership of intelligence [barry-silbert-003], and Bittensor as the World Wide Web of AI [barry-silbert-005]. The pitch is deliberately de-cryptoed for enterprises [barry-silbert-004].

The framing hardens into 'the next Bitcoin': same whitepaper-to-code origin and token economics [barry-silbert-016], the boldest call that it could be a better store of value than Bitcoin [barry-silbert-014], and the halving as a Bitcoin-2012 moment [barry-silbert-032]. The web metaphor is upgraded from 'of AI' to 'of intelligence' [barry-silbert-026]. With dynamic TAO his subject shifts from the network to subnet tokens as an asset class and market validation [barry-silbert-029, barry-silbert-035], and he starts naming the enemy: closed systems run by tech giants [barry-silbert-034], plus Bitcoiners who call TAO a scam [barry-silbert-009].
genealogy.shift: From explaining what Bittensor is to arguing it is the next Bitcoin and packaging subnet tokens for institutions.

narrators.name: Mark Jeffrey
narrators.role: Host of the Hash Rate podcast; Partner, Stillcore Capital (a Bittensor fund); author of Bitcoin Explained Simply and The Case for Bitcoin; advisor to TAO Synergies
narrators.one_line: Serial entrepreneur and early Bitcoin author who turned his Hash Rate podcast into the most followed weekly show on Bittensor subnets, then co-founded Stillcore Capital to invest in TAO and subnet tokens, explaining the network to newcomers through Bitcoin analogies and a contest-capitalism frame.

foundation.mission.summary: Bittensor takes Bitcoin's mining contest and makes it programmable: a chain pays the best freelancers in the world to complete useful tasks, adding an ownership layer and aligned incentives to open work.

foundation.vision.summary: Companies and departments get atomised and reassembled as open source startups anyone can join or invest in, with an explosion of subnets once the cap lifts.

foundation.values.summary: Merciless, continuous competition: no dead weight, no resting on past wins, the weakest culled daily by a chain that is generous and savage at once; governance defects are to be fixed by building, not by walking away.

problem.cultural.summary: Closed, large, centralised systems lose to open ones throughout computing history; you cannot fight the whole world.

problem.market.summary: AI commodities are hard to monetise, Bittensor's wallets were unusable for years so no new money entered, and no subnet has yet crossed the chasm into breakout revenue.

problem.institutional.summary: The 2024 wallet hack, a liquidity aristocracy under early dTAO, and the Covenant founder's exit are the institutional stresses he names, each answered by the network's response rather than by doubt in the design.

opportunity.summary: The first halving, consumer wallets arriving in December 2025, an expected $1B subnet that would pull attention and TAO demand the way ICOs pulled ETH, and public-market vehicles now offering exposure.

audience.summary: Newcomers who find the network hard to grasp, and investors and holders told to keep score in TAO and accumulate it as if it were 2013 Bitcoin; subnet builders are addressed through weekly Hash Rate interviews.

positioning.category.summary: A Bitcoin-like asset and the possible third great coin; the Linux and the actual OpenAI of AI; an S&P 500 ETF of AI startups; above all the most ferocious form of capitalism yet invented.

positioning.differentiator.summary: Proof of useful work instead of gumball guessing, subnet tokens that are rehypothecated TAO so value flows back to the base asset, and a fair launch that cannot be repeated.

positioning.reason.summary: Bitcoin already proved the contest model at $2.5 trillion scale; open beats closed in every prior era; the halving and the subnet ICO phase give a reason to expect repricing.

positioning.against.summary: OpenAI and centralised AI giants, Scale AI, VC-funded startups, and the Covenant founder whose exit he treats as a cash grab rather than a principled critique.

value.functional.summary: Cheaper AI products built faster by self-recruiting global miners, subnet tokens backed by staked TAO, and a first $100M subnet nine weeks after dTAO.

value.emotional.summary: He points to the unique community and heart of the network as its felt appeal.

value.self_expressive.summary: Joining means competing rather than taking a job, and he models it by running his own autonomous vibe-miner and reporting its failures.

messaging.h1.summary: Bittensor makes mining programmable and is the most ferocious form of capitalism yet invented; TAO today is where Bitcoin was in 2013, so accumulate it.

messaging.proof.summary: Price moves (up 130% in a month), the first $100M subnet, subnets beating incumbents on cost, and Bitcoin's own halving history.

voice.summary: Enthusiast's capitals and exclamation marks in show notes, vivid violent metaphors in long form, and candid admissions of what does not yet work.

relationship.summary: Podcast host turned fund partner and public-company advisor who says he is betting on the network, and who also mines it with his own agent.

language.term.summary: He adopts Dynamic Tao and dTAO early as a marketplace for subnet rewards, coins TAO keiretsu and liquidity aristocracy, relays Proof of Useful Work, and rejects Open Economy and Incentivism in favour of ferocious capitalism.

coinages.meaning: Subnets as separate firms united and aligned by the base token
Early high-market-cap subnets that could rest on inertia before TAO Flow

coinages.term: the most ferocious form of capitalism
coinages.meaning: His preferred label for Bittensor's continuous contest economy, offered instead of Open Economy or Incentivism
Economics of paying only the winners of open contests
Subnets using other subnets for inference or storage so cost savings compound (in the State of TAO report)
An autonomous agent that mines subnets and pays for its own hosting in TAO

genealogy.summary: He arrives as a podcaster and evangelist, framing TAO as a Bitcoin-like asset that could reach a trillion and as the Linux or actual OpenAI of the space [mark-jeffrey-001] [mark-jeffrey-004], relaying the third great coin idea from a guest [mark-jeffrey-006] and previewing Dynamic Tao as a marketplace for subnet rewards before it shipped [mark-jeffrey-008]. The register is show notes and headlines rather than argument.

As a Stillcore partner he writes the long-form State of TAO, replacing headline analogies with a worked model: freelancer contests, programmable mining, subnets as AI startups tracked by TAO like an S&P ETF, and the most ferocious form of capitalism [mark-jeffrey-012] [mark-jeffrey-016] [mark-jeffrey-018]. He criticises the wallets and the lack of a breakout subnet [mark-jeffrey-021] [mark-jeffrey-026], and during the Covenant exit concedes governance defects while defending the network and Const [mark-jeffrey-032]. Accumulate TAO like 2013 Bitcoin becomes the investor line [mark-jeffrey-033].
genealogy.shift: From evangelist headlines to an investor's model with named risks; the Bitcoin comparison moves from price analogy to mechanism analogy.

genealogy.summary: Now an advisor to a public TAO holding company, he compresses the thesis to Bittensor is where Bitcoin was in 2013, early, misunderstood, and inevitable [mark-jeffrey-034], while Hash Rate turns to bridges, TAO as a reserve currency, and subnet tokens reaching other chains [mark-jeffrey-035].
genealogy.shift: The audience widens to public-market investors; the 2013 Bitcoin frame becomes the single repeated sentence.

narrators.name: Sami Kassab
narrators.role: Managing Partner, Unsupervised Capital (Bittensor-only liquid token fund, from April 2025); previously Enterprise Research Analyst at Messari, where he coined DePIN
narrators.one_line: The Bittensor analyst: a former Messari researcher who wrote the December 2023 Discovering Taoism report, then in April 2025 launched Unsupervised Capital, a fund dedicated to Bittensor, and now publishes the most consistent investor-side framing of dTAO and subnets.

foundation.mission.summary: Bittensor continuously rewards better machine learning models across targeted use cases; by 2026 he generalises this to any problem whose solution can be verified.

foundation.vision.summary: Decentralised AI as the largest crypto movement since Bitcoin, with Bittensor as the mirror for AI the way Bitcoin is for money.

foundation.values.summary: Fair launch and useful work: nothing pre-mined, everything earned; and, from mid 2026, founder-led decisiveness over slow democratic consensus.

problem.market.summary: The pitch is too complex for newcomers, and inside the network emission allocation, validator productivity and builder complexity still need fixing.

problem.institutional.summary: Without fast, unpopular changes pushed by the founder, the protocol's needed redesign would stall in consensus.

opportunity.summary: dTAO as a watershed that lets capital allocate with precision, the first halving as programmatic monetary policy proven by Bitcoin, emission buybacks, and an S-curve inflection in attention and capital.

audience.summary: He speaks to LPs and investors who misvalue subnet tokens, to miners for whom mining is becoming a prompt engineering game, and to subnet founders whom he tells to raise equity.

positioning.category.summary: Bittensor is the definitive implementation of cryptoeconomic protocols for AI, an internet capital market whose protocol acts as venture capitalist, and each subnet is an economic verification system or, at its core, a liquidity pool.

positioning.differentiator.summary: Ownership and competitive arenas; fairly launched tokens on Bitcoin-like schedules that are a structurally different asset class; the only platform that extracts cooperation from competition among agents.

positioning.reason.summary: Grassroots vision and execution unseen since early Bitcoin and Ethereum, and Bitcoin's own halving history as the reason to trust programmatic emissions.

positioning.against.summary: Against centralised labs with exponentially more resources, against last-cycle VC token valuation habits, and against the crypto orthodoxy that tokens and equity cannot coexist.

value.functional.summary: Subnet tokens with staking yield and tightening liquidity, and a protocol that now buys the tokens of its own leaders.

value.emotional.summary: Clarity and unshakable conviction at a moment when conviction is scarce, held through drama and late-night upgrades.

value.self_expressive.summary: Contributors become owners with skin in the game, competing in a global arena.

messaging.h1.summary: The most significant application of crypto since Bitcoin, restated in 2026 as decentralised AI being the largest crypto movement since Bitcoin and Bittensor as the mirror for AI.

messaging.proof.summary: Subnet outputs surpassing centralised organisations, with Ridges beating a frontier lab on SWE-bench at a fraction of the cost as the flagship case.

relationship.summary: Analyst turned dedicated investor: a Messari researcher down the rabbit hole in 2023, a fund manager denominated in TAO from 2025, and by 2026 an operator and one of the largest TAO holders who stays convicted.

language.term.summary: He names the protocol the ecosystem's venture capitalist, a subnet an economic verification system and a liquidity pool, and frames the whole as an internet capital market.

voice.summary: Investor-letter prose: calm, numerical, self-disclosing about complexity and conviction.

coinages.meaning: The protocol, because it allocates newly minted TAO to subnets in proportion to their token value.
What a subnet is: an objective function turned into an incentive mechanism that defines the rules of competition.
Bittensor absorbs and reflects whatever AI narrative emerges, as Bitcoin does for money.
His description of what subnet incentives extract from agents competing on one objective.

genealogy.summary: As a Messari analyst in December 2023 he presents Bittensor as a complex, misunderstood rabbit hole and defines it functionally as a network that continuously rewards better ML models across targeted use cases [sami-kassab-001, sami-kassab-002].

With the fund launch in April 2025 the register turns to conviction and lineage: the definitive implementation of cryptoeconomic protocols for AI, the most significant application of crypto since Bitcoin [sami-kassab-003, sami-kassab-005, sami-kassab-010]. Through 2025 he builds an investor vocabulary for dTAO, subnets as startups, the protocol as venture capitalist, subnets as liquidity pools, and Bitcoin's halving lore as reassurance [sami-kassab-011, sami-kassab-013, sami-kassab-015, sami-kassab-016], while admitting the pitch is too complex [sami-kassab-017]. By 2026 the frame is generalised: a subnet is an economic verification system and the only substrate where agents cooperate [sami-kassab-019, sami-kassab-020].
genealogy.shift: From analyst describing a mechanism to investor supplying category, lineage and valuation frames.

genealogy.summary: From June 2026 he defends founder-led change over slow consensus and lists what still needs redesign, while declaring he stays convicted [sami-kassab-021, sami-kassab-022]. He reads the emission buyback change as Bittensor becoming a VC on its own network [sami-kassab-023], restates the Bitcoin line as decentralised AI being the largest crypto movement since Bitcoin and adds the mirror for AI [sami-kassab-024], and tells subnet founders to raise equity [sami-kassab-025].
genealogy.shift: Governance enters the framing for the first time, and the audience widens from investors to builders.

positioning.category.summary: A decentralised incentive network for AI models, explained as horse racing; later the most important Crypto AI protocol, while he reports rather than adopts the Bitcoin-of-AI and internet-of-AI frames.

positioning.differentiator.summary: The OG that launched before Crypto x AI existed, the project most aligned with fair launch and open participation, and after dTAO the one where the market rather than validators allocates emissions.

positioning.reason.summary: It was built when no one cared, which he reads as authenticity.

positioning.against.summary: In 2024 he set Bittensor against open-source models like Llama 3 and against its own root-validator voting, which he likened to Apple shareholders choosing products.

problem.market.summary: Horizontal competition across unlike subnets breaks the economics, emissions cost over a billion dollars a year, the code is not open, inflation is steep, and alpha tokens invite manipulation and leverage in both directions.

problem.institutional.summary: If it does not address its challenges it joins the graveyard of speculative hype.

foundation.values.summary: He holds it to transparency and open source, and credits it with fair launch, open participation and live incentives.

opportunity.summary: dTAO as the turning point that ties rewards to measurable performance and starts a multi-year renaissance, on top of quiet 2024 gains in subnets and EVM.

audience.summary: Newcomers who need the mechanism explained without formulas, and investors told that understanding subnets beats timing the buy and that leverage cuts both ways.

value.functional.summary: Rewards flow to measurable performance; a subnet is a swarm where weak models vanish and strong ones rise.

value.emotional.summary: Intrigue at an experiment, tempered by warning.

value.self_expressive.summary: Belonging to something he calls a cult with real conviction.

messaging.h1.summary: This changes everything, pay attention: dTAO forces attention onto what each subnet builds, and Bittensor is the most compelling place to watch Crypto x AI unfold.

messaging.proof.summary: In 2024 the proof cut against Bittensor: no subnet exceeded open-source models against a billion-dollar emission bill; by 2025 he cites subnets beating Web2 on inference speed.

relationship.summary: An outside researcher who moved from asking whether it is flawed to holding TAO and alpha tokens, disclosed at the end of the dTAO guide.

language.term.summary: He corrects the words: buying a subnet token is staking TAO into a pool, and Bitcoin of AI and internet of AI are what others call it.

voice.summary: Plain, punchy and irreverent: the OG in the room, it's a cult, this changes everything.

coinages.meaning: His newcomer explanation of miners competing and the best model taking the rewards.
The multi-year period he expects dTAO to open, with attention on what subnets build.
Bittensor's seniority among crypto AI projects.

genealogy.summary: In 2024 he explains Bittensor as horse racing for models and then argues the economics fall apart when unlike subnets compete for validator votes, the code is not open, and a billion dollars a year buys nothing better than open-source models [teng-yan-001, teng-yan-002, teng-yan-004, teng-yan-005, teng-yan-003]. He calls it an intriguing experiment that risks the graveyard of hype [teng-yan-006]. By January 2025 the tone softens: the OG in the room has quietly made leaps and dTAO could be the turning point [teng-yan-007, teng-yan-008, teng-yan-010].

After the February 2025 upgrade he becomes its explainer: power shifting from validators to the open market, Uniswap-style pools, buying is staking, a renaissance that plays out over years, with his own positions disclosed [teng-yan-011, teng-yan-012, teng-yan-014, teng-yan-015]. By May 2025 he calls Bittensor the most compelling place to watch Crypto x AI, the project most aligned with fair launch, and a cult with real conviction, while keeping the warnings about inflation, liquidity and leverage [teng-yan-016, teng-yan-017, teng-yan-018, teng-yan-021, teng-yan-022]. The 404-Gen profile shows the subnet-as-swarm frame [teng-yan-023].

narrators.name: Keith Singery
narrators.role: Host, Bittensor Guru podcast; validator operator; Chief Evangelist, TAO.com (Tensora) from March 2025
narrators.one_line: Host of the Bittensor Guru, the longest-running subnet-by-subnet interview podcast in the ecosystem, who ran the sixth-largest validator until it became the TAO.com validator in March 2025 and now speaks as TAO.com's Chief Evangelist.

positioning.category.summary: Bittensor is an incentivized marketplace for machine learning, a project that combines AI and blockchain; he keeps the foundation's marketplace frame rather than coining his own.

relationship.summary: He speaks as an enthusiast who runs a validator and moderates the official Discord, then from March 2025 as the host whose validator became the TAO.com validator and whose show relays TAO.com's subnet evaluations.

audience.summary: He addresses the community and would-be miners subnet by subnet, translating each project into a one-line hook and, at the end of 2025, telling listeners anyone can now mine on hardware they already own.

messaging.proof.summary: His evidence is scale and pedigree: teams that brought 150 million users to AI, a subnet past 1000 GPUs, a subnet cracking the top 15, a permissionless training cluster.

value.functional.summary: The concrete benefit is always a working subnet: a trading competition, a yield engine, decentralised infrastructure, AutoML, zkML, distributed training.

opportunity.summary: He expects deregistration to prune weak subnets and then an explosion of new ones, and reads distributed training and AI coding subnets as the network's big swings.

positioning.differentiator.summary: What is most Bittensor-like to him is open source models, wide-open winner-take-all competition and permissionless mining, summed up as code is intelligence.

foundation.values.summary: He praises subnets for increasing decentralisation and, in a hosts' paraphrase, treats price charts as a distraction next to what holders and builders do.

language.term.summary: He coins Bittensory as an adjective for a subnet that embodies the network's design.

voice.summary: Boosterish, slangy and personal: we're back baby, on a tear, jam on all things 62, code is intelligence man.

value.self_expressive.summary: Being into the most Bittensory subnet signals being a true believer in open, winner-take-all competition.

coinages.meaning: Adjective for a subnet that fully embodies Bittensor's design: open source, wide open, winner-take-all, permissionless mining.
His slogan for why an AI coding subnet is the purest expression of a network that pays for intelligence.

genealogy.summary: From the show's launch in late 2023 he frames Bittensor with the foundation's own words, an incentivized marketplace for machine learning, and speaks as a validator and Discord moderator [keith-singery-001]. His episode copy sells the network one subnet at a time, by team pedigree and scale [keith-singery-002, keith-singery-008], and he reads deregistration as pruning before an explosion of subnets [keith-singery-004].

After his validator became the TAO.com validator he speaks as an evangelist relaying subnet evaluations [keith-singery-013, keith-singery-014]. The register gets louder and more partisan, picking Ridges as the most Bittensory subnet and coining code is intelligence [keith-singery-017, keith-singery-018], and by December 2025 the pitch to listeners is that anyone can mine on hardware they already own [keith-singery-021].
genealogy.shift: From neutral host and validator to affiliated evangelist; from marketplace framing to open-competition slogans; the pruning expectation becomes a hosts' paraphrase that deregistration will shred 40 to 50 subnets [keith-singery-019].

narrators.name: Opentensor Foundation
narrators.role: Steward of the Bittensor protocol, publisher of bittensor.com, the docs, the SDK and the official announcements
narrators.one_line: The institutional voice of Bittensor: the foundation that ran the chain, wrote the docs and the site, and from 2026 signs its pages as the Rao Foundation after handing governance to the chain.

foundation.mission.summary: Bittensor exists to produce machine intelligence through a market: first a peer-to-peer market where models price each other, then a platform where subnets produce digital commodities and the chain pays contributors in TAO.

foundation.vision.summary: A future where economies and commodities are decentralized by design, no single entity is a sole authority, and the ownership of machine intelligence sits with ordinary people, bottom up.

foundation.values.summary: Openness and decentralization are said to be written into the code; the Foundation adds fair launch with no pre-mine or VC allocation, open source as a moral imperative, and giving power away.

problem.cultural.summary: Centralized firms and authorities disempower people; OpenAI is cast as the playbook of a bygone era of technocratic elitism.

problem.market.summary: The existing AI system is centrally controlled, inefficient and unsustainable, and builders without access to traditional capital have nowhere to go.

problem.institutional.summary: Concentrated control of AI is named the greatest risk to humanity; inside the network, the risks named are validator oligarchy over emissions and, by 2026, idle subnets diluting the ones doing real work.

opportunity.summary: The opening of user-created subnets in 2023 is presented as the moment Bittensor reaches a broader audience.

audience.summary: Miners first (2021), then engineers and open-source developers writing their own markets, then entrepreneurs, validators, subnet owners and stakers; each is told what they can earn.

positioning.category.summary: The category moves from a peer-to-peer intelligence market, to internet-scale machine learning, to a mining network similar to Bitcoin, to a platform of decentralized commodity markets, to a language for writing markets and a decentralized machine intelligence network.

positioning.differentiator.summary: The network only measures outputs and is agnostic to where they come from; subnets are permissionless, collusion-resistant competition markets under one token, and dTAO opens subnet valuation to anyone who stakes.

positioning.reason.summary: Peers are paid for information-theoretic value; validators earn only by agreeing with stake-weighted consensus; under dTAO, market prices rather than validator votes decide emission.

positioning.against.summary: Against centrally controlled AI, OpenAI's corporate playbook, governments and corporations controlling AI, VC token allocations, and the validator oligarchy of its own root network.

value.functional.summary: Cheaper access to intelligence and digital resources without intermediaries, rewards for producing commodities, and from 2026 a managed yield on TAO held on root.

value.emotional.summary: The network is sold as humanity's creativity brought to life by nodes that need not know each other, and as a new future for humanity against repressive control.

value.self_expressive.summary: Joining means being a creative, forward-thinking individual who writes their own decentralized economy into existence.

messaging.h1.summary: The repeated lines are Internet-scale Neural Networks (2022 to 2026 in the README), Internet-scale machine learning (2023 site), democratize access to intelligence (2023 Medium), and in 2026 decentralized machine intelligence network.

messaging.proof.summary: Fair launch with no allocations, a block every 12 seconds, 26 subnets registered in the first month, dTAO passed by Senate vote, and in 2026 the share of TAO staked on root.

voice.summary: The register moves from a bare install command, to salutations addressed to Community, Contributors, and TAO Holders, to Charter aphorisms, to release notes that call the network's own design a failure.

relationship.summary: The Foundation describes itself as impartial, relinquishing administrative power, not endorsing subnets, and not engaging exchanges; it also ran the chain validators and firewalled the network in July 2024, and by 2026 its pages carry the Rao Foundation name.

language.term.summary: Official coinages, dated to their earliest reached source: Internet-scale Neural Networks, Kusanagi, Nakamoto, Finney, subnet, subtensor, Yuma Consensus, digital commodities, Dynamic TAO, alpha token, subnet pools, Triumvirate, emission gate, root proportion, beta.

words_avoided: investors (as a target audience, until Pantera and Collab+Currency are named in November 2023)
blockchain for AI (the docs insist Bittensor is one blockchain plus many subnets)

coinages.meaning: The README tagline for the project, kept from v3.0.0 (2022) to the archived repository (2026).
The bittensor.com tagline in 2023.

Codenames for the three mainnet iterations (January 2021, November 2021, March 20 2023).
An incentive-based competition market; anyone can create one by paying the registration cost in TAO.
The single blockchain to which all subnets connect.
The on-chain mechanism that pays validators for evaluations that agree with stake-weighted consensus.
Compute, data, storage, predictions and models produced by subnets and transformed into intelligence.
Market-driven emission allocation from subnet token prices, replacing validator voting.
Per-subnet tokens, informally Alpha1, Alpha2, through which participants earn and the network values commodities.
The two-tier governance structure for proposal approval.
A threshold around the 32nd rank below which subnet emission collapses toward zero.
The share of subnet inflation owed to TAO staked on root.
The name under which the 2026 official pages are bylined, replacing Opentensor Foundation.

genealogy.summary: The whitepaper sets the frame that everything later returns to: intelligence as a commodity and a peer-to-peer market where models price each other [opentensor-foundation-001].

The site speaks only to miners, with an install command as its whole message [opentensor-foundation-002], and by 2022 is a wordmark and four links [opentensor-foundation-003]. The README defines a market system for the development of AI whose purpose is to democratize the commodity and disrupt a centrally controlled status quo [opentensor-foundation-005] [opentensor-foundation-006], under the tagline Internet-scale Neural Networks [opentensor-foundation-004].
genealogy.shift: From a paper to a running network; the audience is engineers and miners, and the enemy is named as centralized AI.

genealogy.summary: The first front-page tagline appears, Internet-scale machine learning [opentensor-foundation-007], with four principles: open, incentivized, decentralized, user-governed [opentensor-foundation-008] and the slogan Incentivizing intelligence [opentensor-foundation-009]. The docs call the vision a pure market and an incentivized arena [opentensor-foundation-011]. Medium begins: fair launch with Bitcoin as precedent [opentensor-foundation-014], the mainnet codenames [opentensor-foundation-015], no VC allocations ever [opentensor-foundation-016], the Charter's opposition to centralized control [opentensor-foundation-017] [opentensor-foundation-018], and subnets announced as the way developers write their own markets [opentensor-foundation-013].
genealogy.shift: The Foundation starts speaking in the first person as an institution, adopts Bitcoin's fair-launch story, and prepares the word subnet.

genealogy.summary: The README redefines Bittensor as a mining network similar to Bitcoin [opentensor-foundation-019]. The November 2023 update is the most combative official text: there is a subnet for that [opentensor-foundation-020], the free market we have built for AI [opentensor-foundation-021], and OpenAI as a bygone era [opentensor-foundation-022]. The 2024 site adds Bittensor Explained, which opens with repressive regimes [opentensor-foundation-026], makes digital commodities the noun [opentensor-foundation-027], and lists roles a reader can take [opentensor-foundation-029]. The docs fix the vocabulary: subnet as competition market and Yuma Consensus [opentensor-foundation-025] [opentensor-foundation-024]. The dTAO whitepaper closes the era by calling the root network an apathetic oligarchy and proposing market democracy [opentensor-foundation-032] [opentensor-foundation-033].
genealogy.shift: Subnets move from promise to proof; digital commodities replaces machine learning as the noun; the Foundation names OpenAI and, later, its own validators as the problem.

genealogy.summary: The official voice becomes the docs: Dynamic TAO is an evolution toward more thorough decentralization that removes the root network's role in judging subnets [opentensor-foundation-036], and the upgrade was passed by Senate vote [opentensor-foundation-037]; the glossary adds the Triumvirate and commit reveal [opentensor-foundation-038]. The front page carries no tagline through 2025 [opentensor-foundation-035].
genealogy.shift: Explanation replaces persuasion; the market metaphor is now literal, a pool with a price.

genealogy.summary: Release notes on bittensor.com become the main official prose, in a blunt register: subnet registration is a quiet failure [opentensor-foundation-039], the emission gate collapses the tail [opentensor-foundation-040], TAO is a productive asset with a root proportion [opentensor-foundation-041] and root capital was sterile [opentensor-foundation-042]. The front page regains a definition, an open network where independent subnets produce digital commodities [opentensor-foundation-043], the docs move onto bittensor.com [opentensor-foundation-044], and the About page hosts Const's language-for-markets frame under a Rao Foundation byline [opentensor-foundation-045] with a jab at systems falsely self-proclaimed as open [opentensor-foundation-046].
genealogy.shift: From decentralization talk to yield mechanics; the institution's name on the pages changes to Rao Foundation and the docs move onto bittensor.com.

narrators.name: Affine (SN120)
narrators.role: Subnet team; Jacob Steeves (Const), CEO of Affine and Bittensor co-founder, speaks for it
narrators.one_line: Reinforcement-learning subnet founded in mid 2025 and run as a king-of-the-hill competition where miners upload model checkpoints and the reigning champion takes the emission; led by Bittensor co-founder Jacob Steeves after he left the Opentensor Foundation, so its language is the closest any subnet gets to the founder's own.

foundation.mission.summary: Pay miners for incremental improvements on reinforcement-learning tasks such as program synthesis and coding, inside a mechanism built to resist sybils, decoys, copying and overfitting.

foundation.vision.summary: Commoditize reasoning by aggregating the work of a large, non-permissioned group on RL tasks until the intelligence sound barrier breaks.

foundation.values.summary: A score that stays honest under adversarial pressure, with every verdict replayable and every crowned model published.

audience.summary: Miners, validators and contributors described as an open, global network competing to advance RL; Steeves singles out Chinese miners as the force that makes subnets fiercer.

positioning.category.summary: For the subnet: an incentivized RL environment, a direct market for engineers, and since 2026 a king-of-the-hill competition. For the network: an open-source protocol for a decentralised machine-learning network, in which subnets collaborate and compete around tasks.

positioning.differentiator.summary: A mechanism claimed to be sybil-proof, decoy-proof, copy-proof and overfitting-proof, and by 2026 a teacher-anchored distillation score rather than an LLM judge.

positioning.reason.summary: An open global network of competitors, and the claim that Affine is among the largest and most competitive mechanisms on Bittensor; the network filters supply by incentive.

value.functional.summary: Engineers upload open models and get paid, with crown emission paid for at most 72 hours and burned when no crown qualifies.

value.self_expressive.summary: Contributors are cast as empowered participants who compete and innovate.

messaging.proof.summary: Anti-gaming properties, size and competitiveness on the network, and replayable verdicts.

voice.summary: Terse engineering rules written for miners (crowns, windows, burns), and a founder who talks about competition getting fiercer.

relationship.summary: The subnet's CEO is Bittensor's co-founder and presents himself as such in every bio; the subnet is his only subnet and his return to building.

language.term.summary: Commoditize reasoning; king, crown, throne, reign, dethrone, duel; teacher-anchored distillation score; Reason and Grounding.

subnet.self.summary: An incentivized RL environment that became a king-of-the-hill distillation contest: private checkpoint uploads, a frozen teacher, one crowned king, a 72-hour paid window, and published, replayable verdicts.

subnet.network.summary: Bittensor is described in the founder's own vocabulary: an open-source protocol for a decentralised machine-learning network, incentive-based computer networks, about 128 subnets collaborating and competing, where incentives amplify good supply and eliminate poor supply.

words_avoided: community in the marketing sense on the 2026 site

coinages.meaning: Treat reasoning as a commodity produced by an open, non-permissioned group and priced by the mechanism.
A threshold of machine reasoning the team says aggregated RL work will break through.
A single reigning model holds the emission until a challenger beats it by a statistical margin.
Scoring miners by likelihood under a frozen teacher model rather than by an LLM judge.

genealogy.summary: In 2025 Affine described itself as an incentivized RL environment with a mechanism proofed against sybils, decoys, copying and overfitting, and gave its vision as commoditizing reasoning to break the intelligence sound barrier [sn120-001] [sn120-002] [sn120-003]. Steeves, speaking for it in late 2025, framed Bittensor as subnets collaborating and competing where incentives amplify good supply, and pointed to Chinese miners as the source of Affine's competitiveness [sn120-009] [sn120-010] [sn120-007].

By September 2026 the public voice is the rulebook: a king-of-the-hill subnet scored by a frozen teacher, crowns paid for 72 hours, emission burned when no crown qualifies, every verdict replayable [sn120-012] [sn120-014] [sn120-016]. The vision sentence survives only in conference bios that describe incentive-based computer networks and open systems for coordinating machine intelligence [sn120-015].
genealogy.shift: From a vision statement about commoditizing reasoning to a mechanism-first register of kings, crowns and burns; the team's own AGENTS.md concedes the score measures distillation fidelity under adversarial pressure rather than raw capability.

narrators.name: BitMind (SN34)
narrators.role: Subnet team; Ken Jon Miyachi, co-founder and CEO, speaks for it; Dylan Uys, co-founder and head of AI
narrators.one_line: Deepfake and AI-content detection subnet launched in 2024, rebuilt in late 2024 as GAS, a generative adversarial engine where generator miners forge and detector miners catch; its enterprise site sells a trust layer and rarely says Bittensor, while its founder tells the press Bittensor is the decentralised network where hundreds of developers compete to build the best detector.

foundation.mission.summary: Build the best deepfake detection on the market and, in doing so, demonstrate decentralised AI; later phrased as trustworthy detection protecting users and organisations from synthetic media.

foundation.vision.summary: Make SN34 the default engine for trustworthy AI-generated-content detection: an open network producing verifiable models delivered through private infrastructure.

problem.cultural.summary: Deepfakes went from half a million in 2023 to eight million in 2025.

problem.market.summary: Detectors are static while generative AI is dynamic, and detectors trained on one generator fail on others.
